passages.title: Burnt offerings
passages.summary: God calls Moses from the meeting tent. He gives instructions for offerings from livestock and birds.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Consider what an offering expresses about devotion and willing service.

contextNote.title: An offering divides work between the giver and the priests
contextNote.text: The giver places a hand on the animal before slaughter. Priests then handle the blood and altar work. The instructions make worship an ordered action involving several people. Their attention to preparation prevents the offering from becoming simply a transfer of valuable property.

passages.title: Grain offerings
passages.summary: God gives instructions for grain, oil, incense, and first produce. Salt accompanies the offerings.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Consider how daily work and gratitude can become part of your worship.

contextNote.title: An ordinary food gift also supports sacred work
contextNote.text: Grain, oil, and prepared bread come from the household's food supply. A portion burns, while the remaining portion belongs to the priests. The instructions connect dedication with the support of those serving at the sanctuary. They also distinguish an offering's sacred use from ordinary consumption.

passages.title: Fellowship offerings
passages.summary: God gives instructions for offerings from cattle, sheep, and goats. Blood and fat receive special treatment.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Consider how gratitude can strengthen your relationship with God and other people.

contextNote.title: A shared offering still places limits on consumption
contextNote.text: The chapter permits several kinds of livestock but reserves blood and fat. Giving an animal does not grant unrestricted use of every part. The repeated rule reaches beyond the immediate ceremony into later generations. Worship includes limits on consumption as well as the act of presenting a gift.

passages.title: Offerings for unintentional sin
passages.summary: Instructions address errors by a priest, the congregation, a leader, and an ordinary person.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Consider how your responsibilities change the effects of your mistakes.

contextNote.title: An error by a leader can involve a wider community
contextNote.text: The instructions distinguish priests, the congregation, rulers, and ordinary people. Each category receives a procedure rather than exemption from responsibility. The priest's case explicitly connects his error with guilt among the people. Position changes the consequences and required response, not whether wrongdoing needs an answer.

passages.title: Confession and repair
passages.summary: The laws address withheld testimony, impurity, rash oaths, and misuse of sacred things.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: How do admitting wrong, paying for harm, and changing actions work together here?

contextNote.title: Access to worship includes those with less
contextNote.text: The law changes the offering for people who cannot afford a lamb. Verse 11 allows flour when even birds cost too much. Read these options together. Poverty does not remove someone’s access to repair and worship. The size of the gift must fit the giver’s means.

passages.title: Restitution and priestly duties
passages.summary: Wrongdoers must return stolen or withheld property. Priests receive instructions for continuing offerings.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Consider what practical repair follows an apology or a confession.

contextNote.title: Repair reaches the person whose property was taken
contextNote.text: The instructions name fraud and withheld property rather than only inner regret. The offender returns what belongs to another person and adds a payment. The offering does not replace that restitution. Sacred duties and practical repair therefore appear as connected responses to wrongdoing.

passages.title: Rules for shared offerings
passages.summary: The laws explain priestly portions, thanksgiving offerings, vows, and limits on eating.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Consider how gratitude and promises shape the way you use what you receive.

contextNote.title: A thanksgiving offering creates food that cannot be kept indefinitely
contextNote.text: The meat must be eaten within the stated time. The rule prevents treating a sacred meal like unrestricted private stores. Priestly portions and limits on eating organize who receives food and when. Gratitude takes material form within a shared practice governed by boundaries.

passages.title: Priests appointed
passages.summary: Moses washes and clothes Aaron and his sons. He performs the appointed offerings before the congregation.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: The Church manual connects priestly service with sacred preparation. Consider the duties that follow an appointment.

contextNote.title: The community witnesses the beginning of priestly authority
contextNote.text: Moses gathers the people before washing and clothing Aaron and his sons. Their new role begins through public actions rather than a private claim. The detailed preparation makes their dependence on prescribed duties visible. Standing apart for service does not place them above the instructions they receive.

passages.title: The first priestly service
passages.summary: Aaron and his sons make offerings. Moses and Aaron bless the people. Fire consumes the altar offering.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Consider how preparation leads toward service for the benefit of other people.

contextNote.title: The priest must address his own need before serving others
contextNote.text: Aaron receives instructions for an offering concerning himself before the people's offering. His role does not mean he has no need for atonement. The service then reaches toward a blessing for the whole assembly. The chapter places representative authority beside responsibility for the representative's own conduct.

passages.title: Nadab and Abihu die
passages.summary: Nadab and Abihu offer unauthorized fire and die. Moses gives further instructions. Aaron explains his response to grief.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: The Church manual discusses responsibility in sacred service. Read that theme alongside Aaron's grief.

contextNote.title: Grief creates a question within the prescribed service
contextNote.text: Aaron answers Moses' criticism by naming what happened to his family that day. His explanation concerns whether eating the offering would be fitting before God. Moses accepts the response rather than repeating the accusation. The exchange preserves judgment within ritual duties during an extreme personal loss.

passages.title: Animals and food
passages.summary: God identifies clean and unclean animals. Contact with certain carcasses brings temporary impurity.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: The Church manual studies these rules within Israel's covenant. Avoid treating impurity as a person's worth.

contextNote.title: Temporary uncleanness requires a process rather than a moral verdict
contextNote.text: Some contact with dead animals requires washing and waiting until evening. The rule names a change in ritual status with a defined end. It does not accuse every affected person of deliberate wrongdoing. The distinction matters when reading bodily conditions beside the book's laws about guilt.

passages.title: After childbirth
passages.summary: The law gives periods and offerings after childbirth. A less costly offering is available.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Consider the distinction between a ritual status and a person's moral conduct.

contextNote.title: Childbirth rules govern access without accusing the mother of a crime
contextNote.text: The instructions attach waiting periods and offerings to giving birth. They also allow birds when a lamb costs too much. The mother's ritual return therefore includes an adjustment for limited means. Do not turn these access rules into a claim that childbirth itself is deliberate wrongdoing.

passages.title: Inspection of skin and cloth
passages.summary: Priests inspect skin conditions and damaged clothing. The law specifies observation periods and separation.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: How can a community care for people who must stay apart?

contextNote.title: Inspection makes time part of the decision
contextNote.text: The priest sometimes waits and examines a condition again before deciding its status. Immediate appearance does not always settle the result. These procedures concern access and separation rather than naming a modern disease. The law's categories should not be treated as verified medical diagnoses.

passages.title: Return after cleansing
passages.summary: The law gives rites for a cleansed person. It also addresses affected houses and less costly offerings.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Consider the importance of helping people return to community after a period of separation.

contextNote.title: Return from separation includes provision for limited means
contextNote.text: The instructions describe a person's return after the condition has cleared. They then reduce the required offerings for someone with little money. The process involves restored access as well as inspection. A poorer person still receives a stated path back into the community's sacred life.

passages.title: Bodily discharges
passages.summary: The laws address discharges, washing, waiting periods, and offerings.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Consider how careful distinctions can prevent shame about ordinary bodily experiences.

contextNote.title: Ordinary bodily conditions affect access to sacred space
contextNote.text: The rules concern discharges, washing, contact, and time. Some conditions occur without any stated act of wrongdoing. The closing explanation ties these procedures to protecting the dwelling among the people. Ritual uncleanness here does not mean every bodily event expresses personal moral failure.

passages.title: The Day of Atonement
passages.summary: Aaron receives instructions for entry into the inner sanctuary. Two goats have different roles in the rite.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: The older Church manual connects the Day of Atonement with Christ's work to forgive sin.

contextNote.title: The annual rite addresses the sanctuary as well as the people
contextNote.text: The instructions describe cleansing the holy place from the people's uncleanness and offenses. The building therefore does not stand outside the effects of shared life. Separate goats carry different parts of the rite. The rite restores the people's relationship with God and the sacred space they share.

passages.title: Blood and the place of offering
passages.summary: The law regulates slaughter and offerings. It prohibits eating blood and explains blood's relation to life.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Consider how reverence for life affects both worship and ordinary conduct.

contextNote.title: Blood receives a stated meaning within the ritual system
contextNote.text: The chapter connects blood with life and assigns it a role in atonement. That explanation supports the prohibition on eating it. The rule reaches households and foreigners living among them. Its meaning comes from the chapter's account of life, not from a modern dietary theory.

passages.title: Limits on sexual conduct
passages.summary: God gives laws about prohibited relationships and acts. The chapter connects conduct with the land's condition.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Consider the duties that protect trust and prevent harm within relationships.

contextNote.title: The land becomes part of the warning about conduct
contextNote.text: The chapter speaks of the land expelling people who defile it. This image links household conduct with the community remaining in the land. The warning applies to Israel as well as the peoples it criticizes. Possessing the land does not remove the account's stated conditions for remaining there.

passages.title: Holiness in daily life
passages.summary: God calls for honest trade and care for people in need. He commands love for neighbors and strangers.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: How can love change the way you treat workers and strangers?

contextNote.title: Holiness reaches the marketplace
contextNote.text: This chapter joins worship with wages, harvests, courts, and trade. Honest weights belong beside care for poor people and strangers. A seller can hide theft inside a measure. Fair trade therefore becomes a duty before God. Holiness reaches ordinary transactions, not only sacred spaces.

passages.title: Penalties and distinction
passages.summary: The chapter assigns severe penalties for specified offenses. It calls Israel to remain distinct.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Consider moral responsibility while keeping ancient civil penalties distinct from present Church practice.

contextNote.title: Distinct identity comes with threats of exclusion and death
contextNote.text: The chapter joins the gift of land with demands for separation. Several violations receive severe penalties rather than only calls for personal change. These are commands within the passage's ancient community structure. Reading their seriousness does not require treating them as instructions for private punishment today.

passages.title: Rules for priests
passages.summary: The laws address priestly mourning, marriage, and access to sacred service.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: What duties come with service in a holy place?

contextNote.title: A limit on priestly service does not remove every priestly share
contextNote.text: Some bodily conditions restrict approach to the altar. The same passage still permits eating the holy food. The law distinguishes participation in a specific duty from receiving household provision. That distinction does not erase the unequal access that the rule creates.

passages.title: Holy gifts and acceptable offerings
passages.summary: The laws regulate priestly access to food and the condition of offered animals.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Consider how careful use of dedicated resources can show respect for those who provide them.

contextNote.title: An offering rule also limits how an animal family is treated
contextNote.text: The instructions prohibit killing a cow or sheep with its young on one day. This restraint appears among rules about acceptable offerings and sacred food. The chapter therefore concerns handling living creatures as well as the condition of a gift. A sacred purpose does not permit every possible treatment.

passages.title: The sacred calendar
passages.summary: God names the Sabbath and appointed festivals. The harvest rules leave produce for the poor and stranger.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Consider how worship, rest, and care for others can shape your calendar.

contextNote.title: The festival calendar includes people without their own harvest
contextNote.text: The harvest instructions interrupt the list of sacred dates with a rule about field edges. Owners must leave produce for poor people and resident foreigners. The season's celebration therefore includes access to food outside the owning household. Worshipful time carries an obligation toward people with fewer resources.

passages.title: Lamps, bread, and a judgment
passages.summary: The law maintains lamps and bread. An unnamed man curses the Name and is executed after judgment.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: How can our words honor God? What responsibility comes with speaking about other people?

contextNote.title: A single legal standard stands beside a severe public judgment
contextNote.text: The account moves from a particular offense into rules concerning injury and killing. It states one standard for native people and resident foreigners. That equality of standard appears within laws carrying severe consequences. Read both the common rule and the danger of the punishment described.

passages.title: Sabbath years and Jubilee
passages.summary: God commands rest for the land and restoration in the Jubilee. The laws address land, debt, and servitude.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Consider how care for land and relief of hardship can accompany faithful stewardship.

contextNote.title: Land ownership has limits
contextNote.text: The land belongs to God in this law. Families hold it under that larger claim. Rules for return and release limit lasting loss through poverty. Read debt, labor, and land together. The chapter describes a social ideal, not evidence that every generation practiced it.

passages.title: Covenant promises and warnings
passages.summary: The chapter describes blessings, escalating disaster, exile, and possible return after confession.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: What hope remains after the warnings? How can repentance begin a return?

contextNote.title: The warnings do not end with rejection in exile
contextNote.text: The chapter describes escalating loss when the covenant breaks. It also speaks of remembering the covenant while the people remain in enemy lands. Exile therefore does not become the final word on belonging. The promise of remembrance preserves a future without minimizing the preceding suffering.

passages.title: Vows and dedicated property
passages.summary: The laws assign values for vowed persons, animals, land, and other dedicated things.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Consider whether your promises are informed, careful, and matched by responsible action.

contextNote.title: A vow requires rules for people who cannot meet the valuation
contextNote.text: The chapter assigns stated values to different categories of people and property. Those categories contain inequalities that the text does not hide. A priest adjusts a poor person's payment according to available means. Voluntary commitment therefore enters an organized system rather than remaining an undefined promise.

lds.text: Consider the importance of helping people return to community after a period of separation.

events.title: Bodily discharges
events.summary: The laws address discharges, washing, waiting periods, and offerings.
events.detail: The rules concern discharges, washing, contact, and time. Some conditions occur without any stated act of wrongdoing. The closing explanation ties these procedures to protecting the dwelling among the people. Ritual uncleanness here does not mean every bodily event expresses personal moral failure.
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Consider how careful distinctions can prevent shame about ordinary bodily experiences.

events.title: The Day of Atonement
events.summary: Aaron receives instructions for entry into the inner sanctuary. Two goats have different roles in the rite.
events.detail: The instructions describe cleansing the holy place from the people's uncleanness and offenses. The building therefore does not stand outside the effects of shared life. Separate goats carry different parts of the rite. The rite restores the people's relationship with God and the sacred space they share.
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: The older Church manual connects the Day of Atonement with Christ's work to forgive sin.

events.title: Blood and the place of offering
events.summary: The law regulates slaughter and offerings. It prohibits eating blood and explains blood's relation to life.
events.detail: The chapter connects blood with life and assigns it a role in atonement. That explanation supports the prohibition on eating it. The rule reaches households and foreigners living among them. Its meaning comes from the chapter's account of life, not from a modern dietary theory.
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Consider how reverence for life affects both worship and ordinary conduct.

events.title: Limits on sexual conduct
events.summary: God gives laws about prohibited relationships and acts. The chapter connects conduct with the land's condition.
events.detail: The chapter speaks of the land expelling people who defile it. This image links household conduct with the community remaining in the land. The warning applies to Israel as well as the peoples it criticizes. Possessing the land does not remove the account's stated conditions for remaining there.
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Consider the duties that protect trust and prevent harm within relationships.

events.title: Holiness in daily life
events.summary: God calls for honest trade and care for people in need. He commands love for neighbors and strangers.
events.detail: This chapter joins worship with wages, harvests, courts, and trade. Honest weights belong beside care for poor people and strangers. A seller can hide theft inside a measure. Fair trade therefore becomes a duty before God. Holiness reaches ordinary transactions, not only sacred spaces.
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: How can love change the way you treat workers and strangers?

events.title: Penalties and distinction
events.summary: The chapter assigns severe penalties for specified offenses. It calls Israel to remain distinct.
events.detail: The chapter joins the gift of land with demands for separation. Several violations receive severe penalties rather than only calls for personal change. These are commands within the passage's ancient community structure. Reading their seriousness does not require treating them as instructions for private punishment today.
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Consider moral responsibility while keeping ancient civil penalties distinct from present Church practice.

events.title: Rules for priests
events.summary: The laws address priestly mourning, marriage, and access to sacred service.
events.detail: Some bodily conditions restrict approach to the altar. The same passage still permits eating the holy food. The law distinguishes participation in a specific duty from receiving household provision. That distinction does not erase the unequal access that the rule creates.
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: What duties come with service in a holy place?

events.title: Holy gifts and acceptable offerings
events.summary: The laws regulate priestly access to food and the condition of offered animals.
events.detail: The instructions prohibit killing a cow or sheep with its young on one day. This restraint appears among rules about acceptable offerings and sacred food. The chapter therefore concerns handling living creatures as well as the condition of a gift. A sacred purpose does not permit every possible treatment.
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Consider how careful use of dedicated resources can show respect for those who provide them.

events.title: The sacred calendar
events.summary: God names the Sabbath and appointed festivals. The harvest rules leave produce for the poor and stranger.
events.detail: The harvest instructions interrupt the list of sacred dates with a rule about field edges. Owners must leave produce for poor people and resident foreigners. The season's celebration therefore includes access to food outside the owning household. Worshipful time carries an obligation toward people with fewer resources.
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Consider how worship, rest, and care for others can shape your calendar.

events.title: Lamps, bread, and a judgment
events.summary: The law maintains lamps and bread. An unnamed man curses the Name and is executed after judgment.
events.detail: The account moves from a particular offense into rules concerning injury and killing. It states one standard for native people and resident foreigners. That equality of standard appears within laws carrying severe consequences. Read both the common rule and the danger of the punishment described.
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: How can our words honor God? What responsibility comes with speaking about other people?

events.title: Sabbath years and Jubilee
events.summary: God commands rest for the land and restoration in the Jubilee. The laws address land, debt, and servitude.
events.detail: The land belongs to God in this law. Families hold it under that larger claim. Rules for return and release limit lasting loss through poverty. Read debt, labor, and land together. The chapter describes a social ideal, not evidence that every generation practiced it.
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Consider how care for land and relief of hardship can accompany faithful stewardship.

events.title: Covenant promises and warnings
events.summary: The chapter describes blessings, escalating disaster, exile, and possible return after confession.
events.detail: The chapter describes escalating loss when the covenant breaks. It also speaks of remembering the covenant while the people remain in enemy lands. Exile therefore does not become the final word on belonging. The promise of remembrance preserves a future without minimizing the preceding suffering.
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: What hope remains after the warnings? How can repentance begin a return?

events.title: Vows and dedicated property
events.summary: The laws assign values for vowed persons, animals, land, and other dedicated things.
events.detail: The chapter assigns stated values to different categories of people and property. Those categories contain inequalities that the text does not hide. A priest adjusts a poor person's payment according to available means. Voluntary commitment therefore enters an organized system rather than remaining an undefined promise.
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Consider whether your promises are informed, careful, and matched by responsible action.

guides.title: Leviticus: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Access to worship includes those with less
steps.text: The law changes the offering for people who cannot afford a lamb. Verse 11 allows flour when even birds cost too much. Read these options together. Poverty does not remove someone’s access to repair and worship. The size of the gift must fit the giver’s means.

steps.title: Holiness reaches the marketplace
steps.text: This chapter joins worship with wages, harvests, courts, and trade. Honest weights belong beside care for poor people and strangers. A seller can hide theft inside a measure. Fair trade therefore becomes a duty before God. Holiness reaches ordinary transactions, not only sacred spaces.

steps.title: Land ownership has limits
steps.text: The land belongs to God in this law. Families hold it under that larger claim. Rules for return and release limit lasting loss through poverty. Read debt, labor, and land together. The chapter describes a social ideal, not evidence that every generation practiced it.
